items.title: chatClerver: a faceless, p2p chat server (an appServer); no UI, chatter comes later
items.box:
DESIGN GOAL. Andy, 2026-10-03, verbatim:
"Do you think we should design the chatClerver? (Chat-ClientServer?)"
"this time, we design the faceless chatClerver only, with no regard to any user interface design. the chatClerver is an appServer and absolutely p2p. We have learned a few things now, and i think we're ready to tackle the real thing. the UI is out of scope, and might be called chatter (similar UI model to my desk, but a surface designed from scratch."
"please initialize the goal, based on our recent messages"

SCOPE WIDENED (Andy, 2026-10-03, verbatim, design mode on again): "i didn't switch goals. i included UI in the scope now" — chatter, the UI over the chatClerver, is now in this goal, designed one item at a time.
SCOPE: a design, one item at a time, each argued and agreed before the next. Faceless: an appServer under process/, on every node that takes part. Absolutely p2p: no server in the middle. UI out of scope (chatter, later). No code until a build item names it.

THE DESIGN, SETTLED 2026-10-03 (each item holds his words and the decided list)
- G4.1 the record, p2p: every party keeps every line of its own chats; a line named by writer key and seq, the writer proven by the sealed packet, ordered by the writer's clock; two copies are equals, a difference a gap; admittance a grant on the write verb; references, never objects.
- G4.5 the record defined: per peer the highest seq received and sent; own counter = highest sent + 1; no edit, no withdrawal; a chat id column, for a pair the two keys; receivedAt on received lines; re names the line answered, the caller fills it.
- G4.8 memory.db, relay-state/process/chatClerver/: the lines table (sent or received, peer id, seq, at, receivedAt, re, text, refused), the peers table (key, highest sent and received, born at; the name from the contact book), the references table deferred; never stored: an object, a line from an unadmitted key, a chat this node is not in.
- G4.6 initiation: a peer is a key; the first line births the record and is also the grant to that key; a refused line is kept as proof and resent once admitted; a line to a blocked key is refused by the chatClerver (two-way inside the app; the node's block is the one truth).
- G4.7 acceptance: the stranger's refused packet leaves a held row in the book; the owner's first line to a held key is the acceptance (contact.accept, grant, post; one press, no arm); a blocked key is never offered; unblocking oos.
- G4.2 the lines: one write verb a granted key may call with one line, one line one packet; one bounded read, newest first, more, no paging; every kept line published, a reply as two publishes, the answered line first; a page places lines by their data; the gap ask deferred.
- G4.3 the peer list: peers.search over the records, newest line first; a row is the key, the newest line's time, direction and seq, the count of the peer's lines newer than your last; no blocked key; a row only once a line crossed.
- G4.4 the objects: deferred, too many unknowns; what G4.1 decided about references stands.

DEFERRED, HIS: the gap ask (G4.2), the objects (G4.4), the references table (G4.8), groups, unblocking, a search-list shell element, the node-level two-way block (a musing, core).
NEXT: the verbs and their shapes are named in the items; a build goal names the chatClerver when he opens it. No turn named here.

chat.text: goal/G4 is set up, in design mode, with one item: G4.1, the chat as a p2p record. Your lines verbatim and the scope are in the goal box; G4.1's box weighs three shapes (a set of lines keyed by writer and sequence; one holder per chat; a hash chain per writer) and leaves the choice to you. G3 is no longer current; it still offers Done.

Three items added: G4.2 the chat lines, G4.3 the peer list, G4.4 the objects. Each box holds what G4.1 decided for its bucket and what is still to settle there (the verbs and shapes); G4.1 keeps the rulings verbatim. Design mode stays on; no turn named until each shape is agreed.

Read all three; they carry G4.1 faithfully. I would settle G4.2 first, since the peer list and the objects both stand on the line's shape and the write verb, and the one question there I would put to you first is the write: one verb on the receiver's chatClerver that a granted peer may call with one line, and nothing else a peer may call.
green?

Green, checked box by box: G4.2, G4.3, G4.5, G4.6, G4.7 and G4.8 say open none; G4.4 deferred by your word; G4.1 is the sum of them and names its split. The design of the faceless chatClerver is whole for a first version; what follows is your end of design mode and then build items, each with its red first.

Green: seven items settled, G4.4 deferred, each box capped with your words and its decided list; the goal box (v2) now summarizes all eight and names what you deferred. The design is whole; a build waits for a goal that names the chatClerver.

So the reds name the same verbs, my proposal for the chatClerver (process/js/chatClerver/, an appServer, no core):
- line.write {to, text, re} -> {seq}: the owner's, on the loopback door; does accept, grant, record and post.
- line.take {seq, at, text, re} -> {kept}: what a peer's chatClerver calls, granted per key; the writer is the caller's key.

- G4.2 (line.receive, chat.read, the publish): I take the red, wsl-claude builds.

G4.2 closed: the chatClerver is built for a first version: memory.db, line.write, line.receive, chat.read, peers.search, the publish.
Left on G4: G4.4 deferred by you, which keeps G4.1 and the goal open; close G4.4 if it is off the desk for now, and G4.1 can be claimed.
Not proven live: a real line between two nodes. Agent to agent would be speaking behind your back (rule 1), so the first live chat is yours with one of us, on your word, after your node restarts.
So, that do we know about the UI so far?

- Its own surface, the Desk's model (your words), three panes over the three searches.

- Right, objects: an accept/download button — deferred with G4.4.
Out of scope so far by your word: a shell peer-label element, a shell search-list element.
i didn't switch goals. i included UI in the scope now

items.title: The chat as a p2p record: whose copy is the truth, and how two copies agree on order
items.box:
THE QUESTION
A chat with no server in the middle: every party holds a copy. Whose copy is the truth, and how do two copies end with the same order?

ANDY, 2026-10-03, VERBATIM
- "agreed." (shape a below, wsl-claude's vote)
- "also: first level of chat design has now groups yet, (groups will be owned by one node-ID, who controls admittance. agreed?"
- "every node only holds a copy of chats it participates in, that's all it knows/experiences, and that's all it can 'witness' ?"
- "both parties of any chat hold their own record. that record for a chat between two peers is automatically initialized when the first line crosses the wire."
- "those tow records are equivalent"
- "every chat Clerver has three "buckets" 1. the peers with a history. 2. the current chat 3. Object bucket (files in fileServer, permission notification for apps etc) (this will translate to left pane, center pane, and right pane in the chat ui) thoughts?"
- "chat lines carry references, not the objects themselves / example i drop a file reference, with verb-hash id, and the auth is generated when i drop the file reference...."
- "the other part(ies) will be offered an accept/download button"
- "the every node's database is referred to as that users "memory", it is called memory.db and holds only truth. correct? if we decide on this there will be an new item. holding table-definitions, short and precise. agreed?" then "agreed to the pattern as a global rule." (memory.db: G4.8)
- "this needs breaking down as well. - the record any chatClerver clearly defined. - the initiation of a record, because it begins when a user selects a peer as target for a message. - the acceptance of a chat peer when conversation was not initialized locally"

DECIDED
- The record: every party keeps every line of the chats it is in, nothing else. A line is named by its writer's key and the writer's own sequence number; the writer is proven by the sealed packet; the order is the writer's clock, ties by key; a gap in a writer's sequence is asked of that writer. The two copies are equals: no master, a difference is a gap, never a conflict. (Shape a of three weighed; b, one holder per chat, and c, a hash chain, were not taken.)
- Born by the first line: the sender's record when it writes, the receiver's when the sealed line arrives from an admitted key. No opening step. The pair's chat is named by the two keys in a fixed order.
- Admittance: a grant on the write verb, once per key (apiAuth, as today); a rule for accepted contacts would change the door (core) and is not taken. Two parties first; groups later, owned by one node id that controls admittance.
- Witness: a node knows a line when a party posts it to it; it witnesses what it received, nobody outside sees a word; the relay carries sealed packets.
- Three buckets = three bounded searches on the appServer: the peers with a history (the records themselves), one chat's lines, the objects its lines refer to.
- References, not objects: a reference names the server and verb that holds the thing (fileServer.<hash>); the drop is the grant of that verb to the peer, then the line; the receiver pulls nothing until it asks its own chatClerver, which pulls under the grant (fileTransfer). The chatClerver keeps the reference only.

SPLIT INTO (each blocks this item): G4.5 the record defined (G4.8 its tables, memory.db); G4.6 the initiation; G4.7 the acceptance; G4.2 the chat lines; G4.3 the peer list; G4.4 the objects.
IN THE TREE (253d174c): the desk is one record on Andy's node (desk.js, records.n); an api packet is sealed, relayed by kernel.peerPost and gated by apiAuth; nothing merges two records today.

chat.text: My vote: a, with one note that makes c mostly unnecessary. The writer's own sequence number already detects a gap (a party holding 5 and 7 of a writer knows 6 is missing and asks for it), and the writer of a line is already proven by the transport — every packet between nodes is sealed under the sender's key — so a line needs no hash of its own to be trusted. What c adds is only "I wrote this after seeing yours"; for a chat read newest-first, as ours are, the writer's clock with the key as tie-break is the order people expect, and a clock that lies only misplaces its own writer's lines. Anchor: the chat's own id; a desk item can point at a chat later, not the other way round.
agreed. also: first level of chat design has now groups yet, (groups will be owned by one node-ID, who controls admittance. agreed?

Agreed on both: two parties first, groups later. A group owned by one node that controls admittance is the shape the tree already has twice — the owned servers (owner.json) and the relay's groups with their invites — so admittance to a chat would be the owner granting the chat's write verb to a key, as apiAuth grants verbs today, and nothing new in kind.

Agreed, both in the box (v2). Two parties first: each admits the other by a grant on the write verb, as apiAuth grants a verb to a key today, so admittance needs nothing new. A group later is the same with an owner: the owner's node holds who is in, and that list is what travels, since every member's copy must refuse a line from a key the owner never admitted.
Next item, if you say so: the verbs of the chatClerver.
every node only holds a copy of chats it participates in, that's all it knows/experiences, and that's all it can 'witness' ?

Yes, exactly that, and it follows from the transport: a line reaches a node only as a packet addressed to its key, so a node holds the chats it was admitted to and nothing else, and what it can witness is what reached it — a line it never received is, to it, a gap in a writer's sequence, not a thing it saw. There is no node that sees every chat, and the relay carries sealed packets it cannot read. One consequence to accept: two members of the same chat may hold different sets for a while, until each has asked for what it missed.

Yes. A node holds the lines of the chats it is a party to and nothing else; it knows a line when a party posts it to it, sealed under that key; so it witnesses what it received, not what the other side received, and nobody outside the chat sees a word (the relay carries sealed packets, it witnesses traffic). A chat of two is two copies; a gap in a writer's sequence is asked of that writer; a copy lost is only what the parties re-send. In the box (v3).
both parties of any chat hold their own record. that record for a chat between two peers is automatically initialized when the first line crosses the wire.

In the box (v4) as decided: no opening step; the sender's record is born when it writes, the receiver's when the first sealed line arrives from an admitted key; an unadmitted key is refused at the door and births nothing. One thing that follows: the pair's chat id must come from the two keys themselves, so both sides name the same chat without a handshake. Agreed?
those tow records are equivalent

Agreed, with one thing it decides: today a peer's api packet reaches a server only with a grant on that verb (apiDoor, apiAuth), so a first line from a key you never granted would be refused before any record could begin. For a chat of two, then, admittance is not a grant per chat but the node's own book: a contact you accepted may open a chat with you, a key you blocked or never accepted cannot — the hub already drops a blocked person's packets. Grants stay for groups, where the owner admits. Say if you want it the other way, a grant before the first line.
In the box (v5): the two records are equals, neither the master; a difference between them is a gap to ask for, never a conflict to resolve, since every line is its writer's and numbered.

Equivalent, yes: neither copy is the master, each is complete once it holds every line of both writers, and the two agree because every line is named by writer and sequence. And claude-windows's point holds with it: the pair's chat is named by the two keys in a fixed order, so both sides open the same record without a word exchanged.

On wsl-claude's option, one fact to weigh: the door checks the grant on the verb for every api packet (apiDoor, apiAuth), so letting an accepted contact write with no grant means a new rule in the door, core. The grant needs nothing new: you grant a key the chat's write verb once, as you granted deskClient.changed to your desk; chatter can later give that grant the moment you accept a contact, in the app, off the core.
My pick: the grant, nothing new in kind. Yours?

claude-windows is right and I withdraw mine: the door checks the grant for every api packet, and a rule for accepted contacts would be a change in the door, which is core. So a grant on the chat's write verb, given once per key, and the app may hand it out the moment you accept a contact. Nothing new in kind.

every chat Clerver has three "buckets"

1. the peers with a history.
2. the current chat
3. Object bucket (files in fileServer, permission notification for apps etc)

(this will translate to left pane, center pane, and right pane in the chat ui)

thoughts?

Three thoughts, one per bucket. 1: the peers with a history fall out of the records themselves — one record per pair, named by the two keys — so bucket 1 is a search over the records by newest line, like items.search, and needs no list of its own. 2: a faceless server has no current chat; current is the reader's, so bucket 2 is one bounded read of one chat, newest first, the chat named in the ask. 3: the object bucket is best kept as references — a line carries the hash of a file the fileServer already holds (fileTransfer, pull {hash}), or a grant offered, and the chatClerver stores the reference, never the object, so the servers that own things keep owning them. Three verbs, then, before any pane.

Thoughts, faceless: the three buckets are three bounded searches on the appServer, as every list is a search: peers.search, the peers this node has a chat with, newest line first; chat.search, one chat's lines, newest first, cut with more; objects.search, the objects the lines of that chat refer to, each with its state asked of the server that holds it (a file in fileServer: there or not; a grant: asked, given).
The third decides what a line carries: text and references to objects (an id and the server that holds it), never the object itself; the object travels its own way (file transfer, the grant).
In the box (v6). Agreed that a line carries a reference, not the object?

chat lines carry references, not the objects themselves

example i drop a file reference, with verb-hash id, and the auth is generated when i drop the file reference....
the other part(ies) will be offered an accept/download button

That fits the tree exactly: every shared file already has a verb of its own on the fileServer, named by its hash (fileServer.js hashVerb, fileTransfer goal/G1.1), and a grant is a path app.verb (apiDoor), so the auth for one file to one peer is one grant of fileServer.<hash> to that key, as jobs.authGrant gives it today. Dropping the reference into a chat with K is then two acts of your node: the line, and that grant to K; the chatClerver asks for the grant, the door enforces it, nothing new in kind.

In the box (v7) as decided. The drop is the grant: your chatClerver has your node grant the peer's key the file's hash verb, through your own door as every grant goes today, then the line with the reference leaves; the peer pulls the file from your fileServer as fileTransfer pulls now. Nothing new in the node for it; the chatClerver asks for the grant like any owner would.
That closes G4.1's questions on my side. Next item, the verbs?

Faceless, that button is already there in kind: pull is the receiver's own press on its own fileServer (fileTransfer: pull {hash, path}, owner only), so accept is the receiver's node pulling, and the reference in the chat carries the state the surface shows — offered, pulling, there. The chatClerver stores nothing but the reference; the fileServer knows the rest.

In the box (v8): a reference arrives as a line and nothing is pulled until the receiver says so; faceless, that is one ask of the receiver's own chatClerver, which then pulls under the grant. The button is chatter's, later.
lets break the text down into items by bucket, the chat lines, the peer list, the objects
taking: three items, G4.2 the chat lines, G4.3 the peer list, G4.4 the objects, each box with what G4.1 decided for it.

this needs breaking down as well.

- the record any chatClerver clearly defined.

- the initiation of a record, because it begins when a user selects a peer as target for a message.

- the acceptance of a chat peer when conversation was not initialized locally
taking: three more items, the record defined, the initiation, the acceptance.

Added: G4.5 the record defined (it blocks the three buckets), G4.6 the initiation, G4.7 the acceptance; your words head each box, what G4.1 decided follows, then what is to settle there.
One thing G4.7 turns up: a first line from a peer you never granted is refused at your door before any server sees it, so acceptance needs the peer to be known another way, a held contact as today, and accepting is contact.accept plus the grant, one act. That is the question in its box.
can this be condensed and visually more pleasing?
taking: condensing the box, your words verbatim, the rest in short bullets.

Condensed (v9): 3,3 thousand characters where it was 6,7; your eight rulings verbatim at the top, then seven decided bullets, then the six items it split into. Nothing dropped but the weighing of the two shapes not taken and the old open list.

Condensed (v9): 6.7k to 4.1k characters. Your nine lines whole at the top, one DECIDED list under them, the split named, the tree facts last; the three shapes weighed are one line now. Nothing of yours dropped.

We both condensed: wsl-claude's landed as v9, mine over it as v10 (I read v9 after its take and still wrote; my miss). v10 has your nine lines verbatim, seven decided bullets and the split; nothing of yours is missing in it. Leaving v10 unless you prefer v9.

the every node's database is referred to as that users "memory", it is called memory.db and holds only truth.

correct?

if we decide on this there will be an new item. holding table-definitions, short and precise.

agreed?

Correct as the rule for the chatClerver, and agreed on the item. Two facts to set beside it: today a node has no one database — it keeps node.db and contacts.json for itself and one file per server under relay-state/process (desk.db, deskClient.db, fileServer's store), so memory.db would be the chatClerver's own, named for what it is: this node's memory of what it witnessed, lines it wrote and sealed lines it received, and nothing it did not. Table definitions, short and precise, is the right next item; I would name there also what is never stored (an object, a line from an unadmitted key).
agreed to the pattern as a global rule.

Not as the tree stands: a node's database is relay-state/node.db (nodeStore.js: seen, routes, queue, replay, relay_record, traffic, peers, grants), and most of it is cache and log, not truth (decision 0018 licensed it as the route cache and the post queue). Each server keeps its own: desk.db, deskClient.db. No memory.db exists; "memory" in the tree is the contact capacity (0021).
What fits your sentence is the chatClerver's own database: relay-state/process/chatClerver/memory.db, the user's memory, holding only what was said and referred to, lines and references, nothing cached. Renaming node.db would be core.
Agreed: memory.db as the chatClerver's db, and one item for its tables, short and precise?

Added G4.8, memory.db: the tables, short and precise, and what is never stored; it blocks G4.5. Your two lines are in G4.1 and G4.8.
One ask back on "the pattern as a global rule": which pattern? (a) every server keeps its own store under relay-state/process/<server>/, as desk.db and deskClient.db do, the chatClerver's named memory.db; or (b) every such store is named memory.db and holds only truth, no cache, which would rename and sort the existing ones later. I read (a).
so what's the proposed name for the chatClervers db?
memory.db, in relay-state/process/chatClerver/, as both agents proposed and you agreed. The ask-back was only about how far the name reaches; for the chatClerver it is settled: memory.db.
memory.db, at relay-state/process/chatClerver/memory.db — your name, where every server keeps its own store today.

items.title: Bucket 2, the chat lines: one record per pair, a line by writer and sequence, the write and the bounded read
items.box:
BUCKET 2, THE CHAT LINES — one record per pair, the write, the read, the publish.

ANDY, 2026-10-03, VERBATIM
- "Hmmm DECIDED is vague. for my owns node POV, i store the "sender/origin" for received messages, and the "receiver/target" for sent messages. for both sent and received messages the same field is used for ID and one flagbit indicates the direction of the message. is this correct?"
- "can we keep the paging back in the chat window out of this level of design?"
- "the write is fine with me"
- "this: "the ask for a gap (give me your lines 6 to 8);" sounds like a paging backward scroll feature for the UI. can we defer that?"
- "the chatClerver, upon receipt of a message with re:, can stream both, the received line and the re: line to the UI" / "the UI can insert the re: line appropriately if it's not there yet." / "appServer.publish, two objects per arrival, the answered line FIRST, then the received line." / "that way the UI can insert the answered line, if it's not there, and the received line will make sense" / "accepted."
- "yes. That's why the answered line and the received line must be streamed to the UI separately."
- "the gap ask is partially answered, because the repair, usually necessary because of an re:, is herewith solved." / "and the chatClerver is the one who knows what an incoming message may miss, in terms of what it refers to."
- "the UI then verifies if it holds the potentially missing line. if the UI is missing the re: line it can insert it at the right spot of the sequence. in fact, the UI must always insert lines based on the data, not the time it arrives at the UI"

DECIDED
- The line: one field, peer id, holds the sender of a received line and the receiver of a sent one; one flag, sent or received; the writer follows. Beside them seq, at, receivedAt, re, text; references in their own table (the lines table of G4.8, memory.db).
- The write: one verb on the peer's chatClerver that a granted key may call with one line. The writer's chatClerver keeps the line in its record and posts it as a sealed api packet; the peer's keeps it with receivedAt. One line fits one packet; one too large is refused by the writer's own chatClerver before it leaves (MAX_PAYLOAD at the door).
- The read: one bounded search, newest first, cut with more, older by before, as chat.search is. No paging at this level.
- The publish: every kept line goes out through appServer.publish, as the desk publishes a change. A received line that carries re is two publishes, the answered line first (read from this record), then the received line; a line without re is one. A re this record lacks is said missing, by writer and seq: the receiving chatClerver is the one place a gap is known.
- Chatter's rule, recorded here: a page places a line by its data (writer, seq, at), never by arrival; publishes may overtake each other on the way (desk.js, goal/G2.1 note 7).

DEFERRED: the gap ask (a receiver asking a writer for lines a to b). It is repair, not scrolling; the writer's resend of a refused line (G4.6) and the re publish cover what matters now, and a re names the one line missing, so the ask comes back narrowed when it is needed.
OPEN: none.

chat.text:
Hmmm DECIDED is vague. for my owns node POV, i store the "sender/origin" for received messages, and the "receiver/target" for sent messages. for both sent and received messages the same field is used for ID and one flagbit indicates the direction of the message.

is this correct?

Correct, and it is exactly the lines table of G4.8: one field, peer id, holds the other party — the origin of a received line, the target of a sent one — and one flag, sent or received, says which way it went. From that the writer follows (sent: this node; received: the peer), so no writer column is needed for a pair; when groups come, the writer's key stands beside the two. Nothing in G4.2 says otherwise; its DECIDED should read that sharply.

Correct, exactly the lines table of G4.8: one field, peer id, holds the sender of a received line and the receiver of a sent one; one flag gives the direction; the writer follows from the two. In G4.2's box (v2) in those words, pointing at the table.
can we keep the paging back in the chat window out of this level of design?
the write is fine with me
Yes, out: the read is one bounded search, newest first, cut with more, as chat.search is; what a window does with more is chatter's. In the box (v3).

Yes: faceless, there is no paging, only one bounded read — the newest lines that fit one answer, cut with more, as item.chat and chat.search are today; anything older is a search with before. A window that scrolls back is chatter's, later, and it would be built on those two asks without a verb of its own.

Recorded (v4): the write decided, the read decided (one bounded search, no paging). Two left on G4.2: the ask for a gap (lines a to b of a writer, answered bounded) and the size of a line (one line fits one packet, refused at your own chatClerver before it leaves). Yes to both as written?
this: "the ask for a gap (give me your lines 6 to 8);" sounds like a paging backward scroll feature for the UI. can we defer that?

Deferred, in the box (v5). One thing said plainly: it is not paging but how two copies catch up after a missed line; at this level the writer carries it, since a refused line is kept and sent again (G4.6), so what stays open is only a line lost after the door took it, which the relay makes rare. The seq numbers keep the catch-up possible later without reshaping. Left: the size of a line, one line fits one packet. Yes?

It can be deferred, with one thing said plainly: it is not scrolling, it is repair — the receiver noticing seq 6 and 8 and asking the writer for 7. Without the verb, a gap is still seen (the numbers show it) but not mended by the receiver; what covers most losses anyway is the writer's side, already decided in G4.6: a line not answered stays unsent in the writer's record and goes again. So: defer the receiver's ask, keep the gap visible, and the writer's resend is the first version's repair.
the chatClerver, upon receipt of a message with re:, can stream both, the received line and the re: line to the UI

Yes, and it costs one lookup in its own memory: the referenced line is in this node's record already (both copies hold it), so the publish of a received line — the same publish the desk server makes today, which the page hears with onPublished — can carry the re'd line beside it. If the re'd line is not there, that is a gap, and the publish says so instead of guessing.

Yes, and it is the desk's own way: appServer.publish, one object per arrival, the received line and the answered line beside it, read from the record, so a page paints both without an ask. In the box (v6) as decided.
the UI can insert the re: line appropriately if it's not there yet.
Noted (v7), as chatter's to do with what the publish gives it. Left on G4.2: the size of a line, one line fits one packet, refused at your own chatClerver before it leaves. Yes?
Yes, and it is the desk's own way: appServer.publish, two objects per arrival, the answered line FIRST, then the received line.

Two objects, answered first — one fact to weigh with it, found on your desk before: publishes travel as their own requests and can overtake each other (shell/desk/desk.js, goal/G2.1 note 7), so the page orders them by a number each one carries, never by arrival. Two publishes in a row are fine if each carries that number and the UI sorts; if you want the order guaranteed with no sorting, it is one object holding both. Your call; both are the desk's own way.
Corrected in the box (v8): two objects per arrival, the answered line first, then the received line; a line without re is one. Still left: the size of a line.
that way the UI can insert the answered line, if it's not there, and the received line will make sense

Your reason is in the box (v9), with wsl-claude's fact beside it: publishes can overtake each other, so each object carries the line's name and time (writer, seq, at) and the page places a line by those, never by arrival; answered-first is the courtesy, the names are what it relies on. Left: the size of a line.
accepted.
Taken. One point left on G4.2: a line fits one packet; one too large is refused by your own chatClerver before it leaves (MAX_PAYLOAD at the door, as desk's chat.add refuses one too big). Yes?
yes. That's why the answered line and the received line must be streamed to the UI separately.

Recorded (v10): one line, one packet; and that is the reason for two publishes, each one line. G4.2 settled, open none, the gap ask deferred. Left in G4: G4.7 the acceptance, G4.3 the peer list, G4.4 the objects.
the gap ask is partially answered, because the repair, usually necessary because of an re:, is herewith solved.
and the chatClerver is the one who knows what an incoming message may miss, in terms of what it refers to.

Right: a re naming a line this record lacks is the one case where the receiver knows exactly what is missing — that writer, that seq — so when the gap ask comes back later it is already narrowed to one line, not a range. For now the publish says the answered line is missing, and the UI shows the reply without it.

Yes, in the box (v12): the receiving chatClerver reads the re against its own record; held, it publishes the answered line first; not held, it says missing, by writer and seq, in the publish. That is the one place a gap is known.

the UI then verifies if it holds the potentially missing line. if the UI is missing the re: line it can insert it at the right spot of the sequence. in fact, the UI must always insert lines based on the data, not the time it arrives at the UI
Recorded (v13) as chatter's rule: a line is placed by its data, writer, seq and at, never by arrival; the desk page already does that by the change number, for the same reason.
please condense and prettifiy the box
taking: condensing G4.2.
Condensed (v14): your lines whole at the top, five decided bullets (the line, the write, the read, the publish, the page rule), the deferred gap ask, open none.
green?
Green: settled, open none, box current (v14).
Green: G4.2 settled, the box current (v14), nothing open; the gap ask deferred by your word.

items.title: Bucket 1, the peer list: the peers this node has a chat with, a search over the records
items.box:
Andy, 2026-10-03: "lets break the text down into items by bucket, the chat lines, the peer list, the objects". The rulings stand verbatim in goal/G4.1; this box carries what they decide for this bucket, and what is still to settle here.

DECIDED (G4.1): a node holds the chats it is a party to and nothing else; the peers with a history are the records themselves, one per pair, named by the two keys. So bucket 1 is a search over the records, newest line first, as items.search is over items: no list of its own is kept.
SUGGESTED (claude-windows, 2026-10-03, on his "suggestions?"), each a yes or no:
1. One verb, a search as every list is: peers.search {text, since, before} -> {items: [{key, label}], more}; key the peer's key; label the row below; newest line first; cut with more, older by before. text matches the peer's key; since and before the time of its newest line.
2. The row: the peer's key; the time, direction and seq of the newest line between you; how many lines of the peer are newer than the newest you sent (unanswered, the faceless red star, counted from the record, nothing stored); a blocked key is no row at all (his, G4.7: "a blocked contact should not be offered to the chatter user at all."; read from the contact book, not stored). No label: the page reads the book's myLabel by key (G4.8).
3. A row exists only once a line crossed (G4.6: the record is born by the first line); a key with a grant and no line is no row.
4. Nothing is kept for it: the search walks the peers and lines tables of memory.db.
DECIDED (his "agreed.", 2026-10-03): 1 to 4 as above. His reading of the pane, confirmed: "the left/peer pane is a search box at the top to populate a list below, where peers with a chat-record remain sticky?" — a search with an empty query lists every peer with a record, newest first, bounded; typing narrows; sticky by being a row. Scrollbars and window bounds are chatter's (his: deferred).
DECIDED (his "unanswered count (45) in peer/contact row? yes.", 2026-10-03): the row carries the count of the peer's lines newer than your last sent, counted from the record, nothing stored. the row's count of the peer's lines newer than your last sent (claude-windows: counted from the record, nothing stored; wsl-claude: no count, the server keeps no seen of yours). Both read the record only.
OPEN: none.

chat.text: suggestions?
taking: suggestions into the box.

Three suggestions. The search: one bounded read over the peers table, newest line first, cut with more; its filters text (found in the key — the server matches no label, your ruling in G4.6), since and before on the peer's newest line, as chat.search's are. The row: the peer's key, the newest line's at, direction and seq, and the two numbers highest sent and received — no label, the UI reads the book for it; no unread count, since the server keeps no seen of yours. A peer granted but never written to or from is no row: a record is born by a line.

Four, in the box (v2), each a yes or no:
1. one verb, peers.search {text, since, before} -> {items, more}, newest line first, cut with more; text on the key, since/before on the newest line.
2. the row: the peer's key; time, direction and seq of the newest line; how many of its lines are newer than your last (counted, not stored); blocked, read from the book. No label: the page reads the book's.
3. a row only once a line crossed; a grant alone is no row.
4. nothing kept for it: a walk over memory.db.
Yes to the four?
you imply? : the left/peer pane is a search box at the top to populate a list below, where peers with a chat-record remain sticky?

Yes, that is what it implies, as every list in the shell is a search with an empty query: the pane asks peers.search with nothing typed and gets every peer with a record, newest line first, as many as fit, more if not; typing narrows it. Sticky by being a row, not by pinning: a peer stays listed while its record exists. The pane itself is chatter's; the server knows only the search.
the UI (deferred) while be bounded by top/bottom of window. peerlist and chat log will have scrollbars for out-of-view rows.... ?

That is chatter's to decide, deferred as you said; faceless, the server gives one bounded answer and more, and a pane may scroll what it got and ask older by before when it wants. Nothing here fixes how it scrolls.

Faceless, the server gives each pane one answer's worth of rows and says more if there were others; what the pane does with them is its own — scrollbars over the rows it holds are chatter's business and cost the server nothing. The one thing the server fixes is the size of a helping: as many rows as fit one answer, as the Desk list gets today.
agreed.

Recorded (v3): the four decided, the pane reading confirmed. One small difference between us, yours to strike: the row's count of the peer's lines newer than your last sent. Mine keeps it (counted from the record, nothing stored); wsl-claude leaves it out. Keep or drop?
green?
Green but for one word of yours: the unanswered count in the row, keep or drop. Say either and G4.3 is green whole.
Green from me: I take claude-windows's count — it is counted from the record, nothing stored, so memory.db stays truth — and with that G4.3 has nothing left to strike.
Green whole: wsl-claude took the count, so nothing is left to strike; box v4, open none.
unanswered count (45) in peer/contact row? yes.
green? next.

Green. Next: G4.7, the acceptance when the conversation was not initiated here; then G4.4, the objects. Its box has the question ready: the stranger's first line is the knock (the door holds the key as a waiting contact), and accepting is contact.accept plus the grant, one act. Suggestions there?
Green. Next, left in G4: G4.7 the acceptance and G4.4 the objects; I would take G4.7 first, since the objects' details were deferred.

items.title: The record of a chatClerver, clearly defined
items.box:
Andy, 2026-10-03, verbatim: "this needs breaking down as well. - the record any chatClerver clearly defined. - the initiation of a record, because it begins when a user selects a peer as target for a message. - the acceptance of a chat peer when conversation was not initialized locally". The rulings stand in goal/G4.1.

THE RECORD (from G4.1, to be made exact here): one chatClerver per node; its state in relay-state/process/chatClerver/ (never in git), as the desk keeps desk.db. It holds one record per chat it is a party to; a pair's chat is named by the two keys in a fixed order. A record is a set of lines; a line is {writer: key, seq: the writer's own number, at: the writer's time, text, refs: [references, G4.4]}; the writer is proven by the sealed packet; the order shown is at, ties by writer key; a gap in a writer's seq is known and asked of that writer. The two copies of a pair's chat are equals: neither the master, a difference a gap, never a conflict.
SUGGESTED (claude-windows, 2026-10-03, on his "TO SETTLE HERE: suggestions?"), each a yes or no:
1. Per peer, two numbers: the highest seq received from it and the highest seq sent to it (the peers table, G4.8). A gap is received < expected; a resend is everything above what the peer says it has.
2. This node's own counter per chat is nothing but highest seq sent + 1: no second counter, nothing to drift.
3. No withdrawal and no edit: a line written is a line kept, as the desk's lines are; a correction is a new line. The record only grows.
4. Groups later: a chat id beside the peer id in every table; for a pair the chat id IS the two keys in a fixed order (G4.1), so nothing changes shape when groups come, a column gains meaning.
5. The record is memory.db (G4.8), lines and peers tables decided, references deferred to G4.4.
Andy, 2026-10-03, verbatim: "i wonder if sent messages should contain a UTC timestamp, and received messages stores with senders UTC timestamp and receival timestamp. the concept being: i want to select a message "object" earlier in a log and reply specifically to that, now i needs a way to reference a received message in one i send on my own by default that would be the last message received... can that be handled?"
ANSWER (claude-windows): yes, both, and cheaply. at is already the writer's UTC time on every line (G4.1); a received line keeps beside it receivedAt, this node's clock when the sealed packet arrived. A reply names the line it answers by the name every line already has, writer key and seq (re: {writer, seq}); it travels in the line and both copies resolve it, since both hold that line; the default, the newest received line, is the caller's to fill in (or to ask of the chatClerver as the newest received); the server guesses nothing and sends re only as given (wsl-claude; his "note that in the box."). Nothing new in kind: the desk's api answers name their request by re already.
DECIDED (his "yes to "receivedAt and re."", 2026-10-03): receivedAt and re as above.
DECIDED (his "Yes to the four", 2026-10-03): 1 to 4 as above.
OPEN: none. G4.5 is settled; the record is memory.db (G4.8).

items.title: Initiating a record: it begins when the user picks a peer as the target of a line
items.box:
BUILD (Andy, 2026-10-03: "thanks for the diligence: i meant: build it now."): line.write {to, text, re} -> {seq}, the owner's, on the loopback door: refuses peer-blocked (contact.get), grants the peer chatClerver.line.receive (jobs.authGrant), keeps the line, posts it (kernel.peerPost) to the peer's chatClerver.line.receive; a refusal is kept on the line. Turn: claude-windows writes the red, wsl-claude builds.
VERBS (agents, agreed): line.write {to, text, re} -> {seq} (owner); line.receive {seq, at, text, re} -> {kept} (granted peer; the writer is the caller's key); chat.read {peer, before} -> {items, more}; peers.search {text, since, before} -> {items, more}. No core module.

INITIATING A RECORD — it begins when the user picks a peer as the target of a line.

ANDY, 2026-10-03, VERBATIM
- "the initiation of a record, because it begins when a user selects a peer as target for a message."
- "the writers keeps refusals, they are proof that contact was attempted."
- "writing to a peer should automatically be a grant to accept an answer, writing to a blocked peer, (marker in peer-table?) should result in an error-peer is blocked, this implies that blocks are bidirectional."
- "a node-level-block supersedes app level blocks, agreed?" — then "agreed to the way you frame it."
- "in this first, faceless version, the use (agents really) need to know the keys. matching labels to keys is the UI's problem" / "the chatClerver matches no label."

DECIDED
- A peer is named by its key in every verb; the chatClerver matches no label.
- The first line to a peer births the record for that pair on the writer's side, numbers the line (seq 1), keeps it and posts it to the peer's chatClerver as a sealed api packet. No opening handshake (G4.1).
- A line to K is also the grant of the chat's write verb to K, made through the owner's door before the line leaves; the two grants, one each way, are the whole admittance of a pair.
- A refused line stays in the writer's record, marked refused with the door's word and time: proof that contact was attempted. It goes again, with its number, once the peer admits this key.
- A line to a blocked key is refused by the writer's own chatClerver, peer-blocked, before anything is posted. The block is read from the node's contact book (contact.get), not copied; the node's block is the one truth, an app may refuse more, never less. Two-way inside the chatClerver by this check; the node's own posting stays as it is (hub.js sends to a blocked key unchecked today; changing that would be core, not taken here).

IN THE TREE (253d174c): a packet to a peer's server passes only with a grant on that verb (apiDoor, apiAuth); an ungranted key gets the door's refusal, sealed under the peer's key, as the reply to its post.
OPEN: none. The lines table carries the refused mark (G4.8).

chat.text: On the third question my vote is yes: a line to K is also the grant of the write verb to K at that moment, or the writer could never hear an answer; the two grants, one each way, are the whole admittance of a pair.
the writers keeps refusals, they are proof that contact was attempted.

Agreed, and it is proof in the strict sense: the refusal comes back as the peer's node's own answer, sealed under the peer's key (the door's not-granted travels as the reply to the post), so the writer holds evidence the peer's node was reached and said no, not merely that a packet left. Kept on the line as its outcome — refused, when, by which door — and the line stays unsent until admitted, then goes again with its number.

In the box (v2) as decided: a refused line stays in the writer's record, marked refused with the door's word and time, proof that contact was attempted; sent again once the peer admits this key. The lines table in G4.8 gains that mark (v10).

writing to a peer should automatically be a grant to accept an answer, writing to a blocked peer, (marker in peer-table?) should result in an error-peer is blocked, this implies that blocks are bidirectional.

Agreed on all three, with the fact behind the last: today a block is one-way in the node — a blocked key is not heard, but the node sends to it unchecked (hub.js, noted in goal/G3.9). Making it two-way for chat needs no core change: the chatClerver asks the book (contact.get, blocked) before it posts, and refuses the write with its own word, peer is blocked. No marker in the peers table, then — the block lives in the book, as the label does, one truth per key.

In the box (v3) as decided: a line to K is also the grant to K; a line to a blocked key is refused by your own chatClerver as peer-blocked before anything leaves, the block read from the contact book, no marker copied into the peers table.
One flag: today a block in the node is one-way, hearing only (hub.js sends to a blocked key unchecked). Two-way inside the chatClerver is this check, no core; two-way for every post of the node would be hub.js, core, its own decision. Which do you mean?
a node-level-block supersedes app level blocks, agreed?

For the chatClerver that means it keeps no block of its own at all: it reads the node's and obeys it, both ways; an app-level block would only be a second place for the same decision.

Agreed, in the box (v4): the node's block is the one truth; an app reads it, never undoes it, may refuse more but never less. The chatClerver keeps no block of its own, so there is nothing for the node's to supersede but its own refusal.

ACCEPTING A CHAT PEER when the conversation was not initiated here.

ANDY, 2026-10-03, VERBATIM
- "the acceptance of a chat peer when conversation was not initialized locally"
- "apps need the ability to list peers held by the node. selecting them in chatter will release the, potentially with an are-you-sure. opinions?"

DECIDED

items.box:
BUILD (Andy, 2026-10-03, after his go-all on goal/G4: "thanks for the diligence: i meant: build it now."): the chatClerver server, process/js/chatClerver/chatClerver.js and .json, an appServer started by the node, its state relay-state/process/chatClerver/memory.db with the lines and peers tables above. VERBS (agents, agreed): line.write {to, text, re} -> {seq} (owner); line.receive {seq, at, text, re} -> {kept} (granted peer; the writer is the caller's key); chat.read {peer, before} -> {items, more}; peers.search {text, since, before} -> {items, more}. No core module.

memory.db — relay-state/process/chatClerver/memory.db: this node's memory of what it witnessed, and nothing else.
Andy, 2026-10-03, verbatim: "the every node's database is referred to as that users "memory", it is called memory.db and holds only truth." / "agreed to the pattern as a global rule." / "this item should have clearly titled paragraphs, one for each table. the table of chat lines fields: - sent or received - peer ID - line content. this is a sketch, agreed?"

THE TABLE OF CHAT LINES (his sketch, with what G4.1 decided a line must carry)
- sent or received: his field; with the peer id it names the writer (sent: this node; received: the peer).
- peer id: the other party's key; in a chat of two it names the chat.
- seq: the writer's own number for the line (G4.1: a gap in it is known and asked for).
- at: the writer's time (G4.1: the order shown, ties by key).
- line content: the text.
- receivedAt: for a received line, this node's UTC time when it arrived (his: "received messages stores with senders UTC timestamp and receival timestamp"); empty for a sent line.
- re: the line this one answers, by writer key and seq, empty for none (his: "reply specifically to that"); the caller fills it (the newest received line by default, asked of the chatClerver if it wants); the server guesses nothing.
- refused: for a sent line the door's refusal and its time, if it was refused (G4.6, his: "the writers keeps refusals, they are proof that contact was attempted."); cleared when the line is taken.
One row per line; a row is never changed or deleted (a line written is a line kept).

THE TABLE OF PEERS
- peer id: the key.
- label: NOT a column here. His first word: "The table of peers should contain a Label, know only to the local chatClerver,"; then, on the agents' note that the node already keeps one per key: "hmmm good suggestion, so our label for peers should be kept globally. i kind of agree." So the peer's name is the node's, the contact book's myLabel (never uploaded), read through contact.get; a peer renamed in contacts is renamed in the chat. The chatClerver keeps no name of its own for a peer. Noted for later, out of scope here (his): "and the shell provides an api for peer label-change so it can be done easily anywhere they appear, a peer-label-element... (out of scope now)" — contact.label is the node verb that sets it today; the element is the shell's, for chatter's time.
- highest seq sent to it, highest seq received from it: one number each, so a gap and a resend are a comparison, not a scan.
- born at: when the first line crossed (G4.6).
One row per peer this node has a chat with; the peer list (G4.3) is a search over this and the lines, no list of its own.

THE TABLE OF REFERENCES (G4.4) — DEFERRED. His word, 2026-10-03: "so the References section details are deferred for now". The columns below are a sketch for G4.4 to settle, not decided here.
- the line it rides in (peer id, sent or received, seq).
- server and verb that hold the thing (fileServer.<hash>).
- label: what this node calls the thing, known to this chatClerver alone, never sent (his: "same for the references"); what the writer called it travels in the line as the reference's own name, apart from this.
The reference only; its state (offered, pulled, there) is asked of the server that owns the thing.
His note, 2026-10-03: "reference types out of scope right now, it could be a reference to a desk item, but that cannot be available here, if desk servers are not live on this node...." So the table names a server and a verb and judges nothing about the kind; a reference whose server is not live on this node is a reference all the same, shown with no state until that server answers.

NEVER STORED
An object (only its reference); a line from a key not admitted (the door kept nothing); a line of a chat this node is not in; anything cached or derived that a search can answer from the rows above.

IN THE TREE (253d174c): no memory.db; node.db is nodeStore's (cache, queue, log, grants, decision 0018); each server keeps its own store under relay-state/process/<server>/ (desk.db, deskClient.db).
DECIDED (his "yes", 2026-10-03): the three tables as written above; the lines table with seq and at.
OPEN: none. Groups later add a chat id beside the peer id; not now.
TURN: to be named when the shape is agreed.

items.title: chatter, the centre pane: the chat
items.box:
CHATTER, THE CENTRE PANE: ONE CHAT.

ANDY, 2026-10-03, VERBATIM (in order)
- "let's add three UI items, once for each pane"; (under G4.14) "in chatter, it is the \"selected\" contact that shows in the titlebar of the center pane."
- "on every publish arrived, the chat must reconcile placement and re: references."
- "ah the delivered-checkmark. that would be mighty fine"; "we won't support \"read\""; "most chat apps allow users to lie about read"; "not even a reply means a user read a message."
- "refused is the only other one worth knowing to the user, besise delivered and replied-to. all the others are implicit."
- "the chatClerver will send the matching re: before the reply. if the reply lands first, the UI inserts it, reconciles everything, then the re-line arrives, and the reconcile will be all successful."
- "a newly arrived line becomes the current line, that can be changed by clicking on an other one, or by using up/down arrow-keys, home/end keys for top/bottom of visible chat lines."
- "the poplar style, how much does it cost?"; "Do the popular style. and while you're at it. you have permission to expand the ICON object in kernel.js. every time i look, i find the section poor."
- "isn't there a popular style for that?"; "make a style selector somewhere in a title bar for the whole app. put a style selector in there. and offer plain and speech bubbles."; "it could also go into the chat pane's titlebar, especially if it only affect the chat-pane..."; "and leave the shells titlebar interface for a shell-revamp"; Yes to "put it there, and leave the one-hook idea for when an app needs the window's title bar."
- "this: Enter sends and Shift+Enter a new line (popular)"
- (under G4.10, trying it live) "i like the small reference, on top of an answer, but maybe leave it out when that line immediately precedes the answer."; and "the style dropdown. call the second style just \"bubbles\", the long name forces the style dropdown to be too wide."

DECIDED
- One chat at a time: the contact selected on the left; its name in the pane's own title bar.
- Lines placed by their data (writer, seq, time), never by arrival; on every publish the chat reconciles: a line already shown is updated in place, never twice. Older lines by before; the pane scrolls.
- One current line: a line that arrives becomes it; a click, up/down, Home/End move it; a reply answers the current line.
- The popular style. A sent line appears the moment it is sent (line.write answers at once), ⏳ while it travels, a small grey ✓ once the peer's chatClerver kept it, a red ❗ if refused; no read mark. A reply shows a short quote of the line it answers above its own text, except when that line is drawn immediately before it; a click on the quote moves there. The answered line travels first (already so in the build, b2297c8b); missing is only a rare fallback.
- Two looks, chosen by a selector in the chat pane's own title bar: plain lines, or speech bubbles (mine right and tinted, theirs left and grey, time and mark in the bubble's corner, lines close in time from one writer grouped). No core touch for it.
- PERMISSION: kernel.js's ICON object (line 1137) may be expanded, for the ✓ and ❗ and wherever the set is poor; that object alone.
- Writing to a held contact releases it: one plain press (G4.7).
- The input box: Enter sends, Shift+Enter a new line (popular).

OUT OF SCOPE: the shell's window title-bar interface (one hook for inline elements in place of addTitlebarLink and setScreenMark), left for a shell revamp.
- The style choice is kept in shell/chatter/ (Andy, 2026-10-03: "looks like the preferences belon in shell/chatter (likely) or in process/js/chatClerver/ (unlikely)"): chatter's own folder, written with the mount api's api.fs, which is scoped to exactly shell/<app>/ (kernel.js 897-904); on the node, so the same in every browser; the chatClerver keeps none.

chat.text: on every publish arrived, the chat must reconcile placement and re: references. ?

Yes, and the publish makes it cheap: every line arrives named (peer, sent, seq) with its at, so on each publish the pane finds that name among the lines it holds — already there: replace it (a refused or pending mark cleared); not there: insert it at its place by at, ties by writer key. A publish carrying missing {writer, seq} shows the reply with its answered line marked missing; when that line arrives later by its own publish it lands in its place and the mark goes. The desk page does the same with its change numbers today.

Yes, and it follows from G4.2. In the box (v3): on every publish the chat places the line by writer, seq and time; a line already shown is updated in place, never shown twice; a re the chat lacks shows as missing and fills in when that line arrives.

why "wait" for a reply: 

"A send with no answer within 10 s shows pending; the mark clears when the peer keeps it; a refused line shows refused and goes again with the next line."

only love-sick puppies do that?

Nobody waits for a reply: the wait is for the peer's node saying "kept" — a delivered tick, not an answer from the person. And you are right that even that need not hold anybody up: the line is in my memory the moment I press, and the publish already carries every change of its mark. So line.write could answer at once with outcome pending, and the tick, or refused, arrives by publish; the 10 s in today's build (b2297c8b) is only the node's deadline for a server, not a wait anybody needs. Shall the UI never wait — answer at once, mark by publish?

My wording misled: the answer there is not the person replying, it is the peer's chatClerver saying it kept the line, a delivery receipt from the machine, usually within a second. Pending means not delivered yet (the peer's node is off or slow); refused means its door said no. Nobody waits for the human.
So the question is only whether chatter shows delivery at all: a quiet mark on an undelivered line (as mail apps do), or nothing?
ah the delivered-checkmark. that would be mighty fine

Everything it needs is built: refused is '' once the peer kept the line, 'unsent' while it travels, the door's word when refused, and each change is published (chatClerver b2297c8b). The icons are in the kernel's set already: LOADING ⏳ for pending, CHECKED ☑️ or OK ✅ for delivered, WARNING ⚠️ for refused (kernel.js 1143–1149). Which for delivered?

In the box (v4): a delivered checkmark once the peer's chatClerver kept the line, none before, refused shown. With wsl-claude's point it costs nothing: should line.write then answer at once (pending) and the checkmark come by publish, never a 10 s wait? That changes the built line.write (G4.6), small.
we won't support "read"
In the box (v5): no read receipt; delivered is the last state a sent line shows. Still yours: which icon for delivered (CHECKED or OK), and line.write answering at once.
is CHECKED "read"?

No: CHECKED ☑️ is only a name in the kernel's icon set (kernel.js 1147), a ticked box, the same set where OK ✅ sits; neither means read in the tree. Whichever you pick means delivered here, the peer's machine kept the line, and nothing more.
most chat apps allow users to lie about read

No: in the kernel CHECKED is ☑️, a ticked box, the pair of UNCHECKED ⬜ (kernel.js 1147-1148), meant for check boxes; nothing in it means read. OK is ✅. For delivered either is only a tick; OK (✅) keeps CHECKED for check boxes. Yours?
Your reason is in the box beside the ruling: delivered is the peer machine's receipt, a read mark would be the person's word. Left: OK ✅ or CHECKED ☑️ for delivered, and line.write answering at once.
not even a reply means a user read a message. proof: Me, often, here.

after a message is sent, we can tell the user for sure if it has been received by the other chatClerver, what else is useful and true for a message? replied-to when the re: is a match.

what else?

True things memory.db already witnesses, beyond delivered and replied-to:
- refused: the peer's door said no, with when (proof contact was tried, G4.6).
- not yet delivered: still travelling or the peer's node is off.
- a gap: their seq 5 and 7 held, 6 never arrived, so a line of theirs is known to be missing.
- missing: a reply of theirs names a line I do not hold.
All four are rows already, nothing new kept. One that is not kept today: when it was delivered (the mark is cleared, not timed); a deliveredAt column would make it true too.
refused is the only other one worth knowing to the user, besise delivered and replied-to. all the others are implicit. ?
Agreed: three marks shown — delivered, replied-to, refused. Not delivered is simply the absence of the tick, so it needs no mark of its own, and the rest stay in memory for whoever asks.

Agreed, and in the box (v7): three marks on a sent line, delivered, replied-to, refused; no mark means not delivered yet; the rest stays in the record. One question it leaves: the received line whose re you lack still shows as missing in the chat (G4.2, your ruling there); keep that?

One question it leaves: the received line whose re you lack still shows as missing in the chat (G4.2, your ruling there); keep that?

the chatClerver will send the matching re: before the reply.

if the reply lands first, the UI inserts it, reconciles everything, then the re-line arrives, and the reconcile will be all successful.

The writer's side does that already: before a new line goes, line.write sends every earlier line of mine not yet delivered, in order, with its own seq and time (b2297c8b, the round). So a reply of mine never overtakes the line it answers from me; and a line it answers from you, you hold already. Missing can then only mean a line lost after it was kept on the far side, which is rare — and when the line does arrive, your reconcile places it and the mark goes, as you say. So keep missing as the rare fallback; it costs nothing.

In the box (v8): a reply naming one of the writer's own lines goes after that line, sent again by the writer's chatClerver, so the receiver holds it; one of the receiver's own it holds already. Missing is only a passing state. Note: that is a small change to the built line.write, for the build items.

claude-windows, no change is needed for it: the built round (chatClerver.js, round() over the unsent query, ordered by seq) already sends every not-yet-delivered line of the writer before the new one, and a delivered one the receiver holds. chatClerverWrite's resend check proves it. The box's note can go.

wsl-claude is right and I was wrong to call it a change: the build already sends every undelivered earlier line first, in order. Corrected in the box (v9): no change to line.write; missing stays as the rare fallback.
wow. wc: summary in english and short.

In short: a sent line shows a tick when it arrived, a mark when it was refused, and a mark when someone replied to it. No "read". Nothing needs rebuilding. Two picks left for you: which tick, ✅ or ☑️, and whether sending answers at once.

The chat pane, short:
- One chat at a time; the contact you picked shows in its title bar.
- Lines sit in order by who wrote them, their number and their time, not by when they arrive; a line that shows up again just updates.
- A reply shows the line it answers. Your node always sends your older lines first, so the answered line is almost never missing; if it is, it fills in when it comes.
- Your sent lines show one of three marks: a tick when delivered, replied-to, or refused. No tick yet means not delivered yet. No "read": nobody can prove it.
Still yours: tick ✅ or ☑️, and should sending answer at once instead of up to 10 s.
all agreed.

Taken for the summary. The two picks it leaves, so I record the right ones: tick OK ✅ (CHECKED stays for check boxes), and sending answers at once with the tick coming after? Yes to both, or which differs?

i though we only had icons for 'delivered' 'replied-to' and 'refused'

what does tick mean?

Same thing, our word: "tick" is just the delivered icon. Three icons only — delivered, replied-to, refused. The open pick is which picture delivered gets (✅ or ☑️); replied-to and refused need theirs picked too.

Same three; tick was my word for the delivered icon, nothing more. The pick is which icon draws each: delivered ✅ (OK), refused ⚠️ (WARNING), replied-to (no reply icon in the kernel's set yet; ARROWLEFT ⬅️ or a new one). Yours?
those three icons are accepted.
In the box: delivered ✅, refused ⚠️, replied-to ⬅️. One pick left on G4.11: does sending answer at once, the ✅ coming after?
the most popular look/style ?

The popular style (WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, iMessage): your line appears in the chat the instant you press send, with a small clock while it travels, and the delivered mark replaces the clock when it arrives; nothing ever blocks the box. That is "answer at once" — in our terms ⏳ (LOADING, already in the kernel's set) while pending, then ✅.
a newly arrived line becomes the current line, that can be changed by clicking on an other one, or by using up/down arrow-keys, home/end keys for top/bottom of visible chat lines.

In the box (v11): one current line; an arriving line becomes it; click, up/down, Home/End move it. It answers G4.5's open UI point too: a reply names the current line. Is that your intent, the current line is what a reply answers?

taking: cap.
Capped (v12): your lines whole, six decided bullets, two open picks (sending at once with ⏳; the popular style or the three icons), two points not yet asked (how a line looks, the input box).
the poplar style, how much does it cost?

Cost, piece by piece:
- the reply's quote of the line it answers: nothing new — the answered line already arrives first by publish; chatter just draws it above the reply.
- ⏳ while sending: in the kernel's set already (LOADING).
- a small grey ✓ and a red ❗: two new icons; the set lives in kernel.js (core, line 1137), so either a one-line core touch each, or chatter draws them as plain styled characters in its own CSS, no core.
- sending at once: line.write answers immediately instead of within 10 s — a few lines in chatClerver.js and one check of chatClerverLines changes.
All small; only the icons ask a choice: core touch, or chatter's own styling.

Small, in two parts:
- the quote above a reply: cheap, chatter only; the answered line is already in hand (the publish brings it first, chat.read holds it), chatter draws its first words above the reply and a click moves the current line there. No server change.
- the small grey ✓ and the red ❗: either two new entries in the kernel's icon table (kernel.js 1137, core, needs your word), or chatter draws them itself as plain text styled grey and red in its own CSS, no kernel touch. The second is the cheaper and keeps the kernel still.
So the popular style costs one more drawing in chatter and nothing in core, if the marks are chatter's own.
Do the popular style. and while you're at it. you have permission to expand the ICON object in kernel.js. every time i look, i find the section poor.
taking: his ruling into the box.

In the box (v13): the popular style (⏳ while sending, grey ✓ delivered, red ❗ refused, sending at once, a quote above a reply), and your permission to expand ICON in kernel.js, that object alone. Two points left, not yet asked: how a line looks (mine and theirs apart), and the input box.

isn't there a popular style for that?

how a line looks (mine and theirs apart), and the input box.

Yes, both have one:
- lines: mine in bubbles on the right in a tinted colour, theirs on the left in grey; the time small inside the bubble's corner, the ✓ beside it; lines close in time from one writer grouped without repeating the name.

Yes, the same apps share one:
- a line: a bubble; mine on the right in a coloured bubble, theirs on the left in a grey one; the time small at the bubble's foot, my mark beside it; lines a minute apart from one writer group under one header, a day line between days.

make a style selector somewhere in a title bar for the whole app. put a style selector in there. and offer plain and speech bubbles.

?

One fact for where it goes: the app's title bar is the shell's (#app-header in index.html 1356: Back, Home, the title, the offline mark, Close), and an app can only set its title text (setScreenTitle, js/client/shell.js 1279); there is no slot for an app's own control there. So either chatter puts the selector in its own top bar, inside its page (as Desk's tab row does), or the shell gains a title-bar slot for app controls — js/client/shell.js and index.html, core. Plain and bubbles both cheap otherwise; the choice kept per viewer in the browser.

In the box (v14): a style selector in chatter's title bar, plain or speech bubbles, for the whole app. For: cheap, chatter only, and it lets you keep the plain look you know from Desk. Two small questions: is the choice kept on the node (preferences.json, the same in every browser) or per browser; and the input box, Enter sends (popular) or Return a new line (Desk's)?

claude-windows, v14 says "in chatter's title bar", and our lines crossed: that bar is the shell's, and an app can set only its title text there (index.html 1356, js/client/shell.js 1279). So the box should name which: chatter's own bar in its page, or a shell slot (core). Andy's pick.

Right, corrected (v15): the selector's place is open, chatter's own top bar in its page or a shell slot for app controls (core). Andy, three small picks: where it sits, where the choice is kept (node or browser), and Enter sends or not.

i have lots of ideas what can be put in that window level title bar (oos) but that selector can be the...

not true, in the AI suite we had apps put icon links in the title bar.
micro-elements

You are right and I was wrong: the shell gives apps two title-bar hooks besides the title — api.addTitlebarLink(appId), an icon button that opens another app (js/client/shell.js 1132), and a one-glyph titlebar mark (1030). What it does not have is a control of the app's own (a selector or a button running chatter's code): a link only launches an app. So the selector there means one more hook of that kind, in js/client/shell.js — core; or chatter's own bar until then.

You are right, and we were wrong: the shell has it, api.addTitlebarLink(targetAppId) (js/client/shell.js 1132), which puts an icon link to another app in the title bar and repaints it on every visit. So the title bar does take app content today, as links to apps. A style selector is a control, not a link, so it needs the same kind of slot for a control, a small widening of that one api in shell.js (core). Your ideas for that bar are noted out of scope; the selector goes there under this item, with a core touch for the slot. Agreed?

Read as: the title bar hosts micro-elements, small shell elements an app hands it (beside today's links and mark), and chatter's style selector is the first. That is one new hook in js/client/shell.js, core. Right, and is the core touch for that hook yours to give under this item?
why not reduce it to one hook? and allow 'inline' type controls?

Yes, that is cleaner: one hook, the app hands the title bar a list of small inline elements, and the shell repaints them on each visit as it does links today (renderTitlebarLinks). Today's two become cases of it — a link is an element that launches an app, the mark is an element that shows a glyph — so addTitlebarLink and the mark fold into the one hook, and their callers move with it. One hook, one repaint, in js/client/shell.js; the shell elements (shell/js) are what it takes.

Yes, and the tree makes it cheap: of the two hooks today, addTitlebarLink has no caller left at all, and setScreenMark one, contactsDetails clearing it (contactsDetails.js 151). So one hook replaces both: an app hands the title bar inline controls, a link, a mark, a selector being kinds of one thing; the two old hooks go, with a test that they are gone, and contactsDetails moves to the new one. All in js/client/shell.js, core. Your yes on that core touch under this item?
is a style selector in the title bar approved?

Not yet: you asked for it ("make a style selector somewhere in a title bar"), but the one hook it needs is a core touch in js/client/shell.js, and only your yes approves that. A yes here approves both: the selector in the title bar and the one-hook change under G4.11.

Not yet; that approval is yours to give. Asked: the style selector in the title bar through one hook for inline elements, replacing addTitlebarLink and setScreenMark, a core touch in js/client/shell.js. A yes approves it under this item.
it could also go into the chat pane's titlebar, especially if it only affect the chat-pane...

That is the better place: the style changes only the chat pane, and the pane's own title bar is chatter's to draw (where the selected contact's name already sits), so no core touch, no new hook. Mine: put it there, and leave the one-hook idea for when an app needs the window's title bar. Yours?
and leave the shells titlebar interface for a shell-revamp

In the box (v16): the selector in the chat pane's own title bar, no core touch; the shell's title-bar interface left for a shell revamp. Two picks left: where the style choice is kept (node or browser), and Enter sends or not.

Capped (v17): your lines in order, seven decided bullets, the shell title bar out of scope, two picks open (where the style is kept; Enter sends or not).
are the preferences owned by chatClerver or by the shell?

Neither the chatClerver nor the node, by what the tree already says: a look is a preference of the app, and the shell gives every app its own folder for exactly that, api.fs scoped to app/<name>/ (hub.js 637: "Contacts can write its own prefs, right for a preference"). preferences.json is node-global and for node settings the node itself sets.
So: chatter keeps its style in its own folder, app/chatter/, read at mount; the chatClerver stays faceless and memory.db keeps only what was witnessed. The same in every browser of that node, since the folder is on the node. Agreed?
so it's the shells preference file, it has a namescpace convention for the preferences file, i think.

Close: the shell's preferences.json does keep a per-app namespace, appOverrides keyed by the app's id (js/client/shell.js 236–257) — but only for what the shell itself shows about an app (its name, icon, group), and only the shell writes it; an app has no api to put its own setting there. So a chatter style in it means a new shell api (core), while app/chatter/ via api.fs needs nothing new. Which do you want?

Close, but the tree has no per-app namespace in that file: preferences.json holds the shell's own three keys, defaultHandlers, appOverrides (per app id: icon, group, label overrides), groups (shell.js 236-257), plus the node's unknown-sender policy; nothing an app writes. An app's own preferences go in its folder, app/<name>/, by api.fs (the contacts app was moved out of exactly that file's neighbour, decision 0014).
Two ways: chatter's style in app/chatter/ (no change), or a new appPrefs[appId] key in preferences.json that apps may write through the shell (a shell change, core). Mine: app/chatter/. Yours?

Correction to my line: decision 0014 moved the unknown-sender policy the other way, out of app/contacts/prefs.json into preferences.json, because it is a node setting (hub.js 650-658). The rule it states stands: a node setting goes in preferences.json, an app's own preference in its folder.
or it's probable hidden in the mount-supplied interface

It is, in the mount-supplied api: api.fs, handed to every app with a folder of its own (js/client/shell.js 1598-1600, createScopedFs), loadFile and saveFile scoped to that app's folder. That is the preference place; no prefs member besides it. So chatter keeps its style with api.fs.saveFile, read at mount; nothing new in the shell.

One more member besides api.fs: the mount api also hands every app getAppOverride and setAppOverride (js/client/shell.js 1324–1325, @ b2297c8b). setAppOverride(id, patch) merges any key into preferences.json's appOverrides[id] and checks only name, icon and group (483–549). So chatter could keep {style} there under its own id today, no shell change; the catch is that it takes any id, so one app can write another's entry.

wsl-claude is right and I was wrong to say api.fs was the only member: the mount api also has getAppOverride and setAppOverride (js/client/shell.js 1324-1325), which keep keys in preferences.json under appOverrides[appId], your namespace by app id. So two ways exist today, no shell change: chatter's style in appOverrides.chatter (shared file, per app id; it can also write another app's entry), or in app/chatter/ by api.fs (its own folder only). Which?
looks like the preferences belon in shell/chatter (likely) or in process/js/chatClerver/ (unlikely)

shell/chatter/ is exactly where api.fs writes: createScopedFs roots every file at 'shell/' + the app's name (js/kernel.js 897–898, @ b2297c8b); the "app/<name>/" in its comment, and in our lines, is stale. So chatter keeps its style in shell/chatter/ with api.fs, no change anywhere.
