items.title: Shell element: the peer label (a peer's name by key, renamed where it appears)
items.box:
SHELL ELEMENT: THE CONTACT LABEL — a contact's name by key, renamed where it appears.

ANDY, 2026-10-03, VERBATIM
- "Let's add two more item's for (new-in-scope) the shell elements needed. - peer label element - peer pane element"
- "the element has two modes, and it follows the style of its container / 1. display only, for insertion in a text flow, or labeling in a table, etc... it cannot be clicked on or modified. / 2. in headings for panes and dialogs dedicated to that peer, when clicked, it offers a text input with label-constraints which updates, if return is hit on the keyboard, and the string is not empty."
- "label have a may length in the peer data" / "labelRule.js" (since renamed fieldRules.js, G4.16)
- (earlier aside) "the shell provides an api for peer label-change so it can be done easily anywhere they appear, a peer-label-element"

DECIDED
- It names no rule of its own: it shows the contact book's caption by key, which the node already decides (wsl-claude's preamble, his "that makes a good pre-amble"): your own name (myLabel) if set, else the peer's own (publicLabel), else the key's tail; the tail added where two names read alike (hub.js contactLabel, 404-416). It arrives with contact.get and contact.search; myLabel never leaves the node.
- It takes the style of its container. Two modes: display only (in text or a table, not clickable); and in headings of panes and dialogs for that contact, a click offers a text input; Return saves it when not empty.
- Mode 2 checks what is typed with js/fieldRules.js (G4.16: a label at most 64 bytes, no invisible or control characters, spaces folded) and says why it refuses, then asks contact.label {publicKey, myLabel} on the owner's door. The node checks it too, once G4.16 brings contact.label under fieldRules.
- It lives in shell/js/ with the other elements (G4.14). G4.16 blocks it.

- It listens for changes in both modes (Andy, 2026-10-03: "the label listens to changes in both modes."): a rename anywhere redraws every label showing that contact.
IN THE TREE (wsl-claude): the node's one event stream (/api/events, server.js 228-272) carries jobs, packets and relay events, nothing about the contact book; contact.label (hub.js 1703) answers its caller and announces nothing. So a label can listen only once contact.label emits a change on that stream: one new event kind, core.
PERMISSION (Andy, 2026-10-03: "it's loopback, it can take it", then "yes. core touch allowed for rename event"): core may be touched under this item for the rename event alone: contact.label emits a contact change on /api/events, and every contact label listens for it.
NAMED (Andy, 2026-10-03: "it has to be aaa contact rename event. Files have rename too, appServers need their name space for streams and the node has its own, hopefully."): the event is a contact rename, named so, not a bare "rename": files rename too, and app servers and the node each need their own names on the stream. IN THE TREE: the stream's events are named job-updated, job-deleted, relay-event, packet, snapshot (server.js 236-270); no namespace rule is written down; app servers publish through jobs.update as {app} today, not as their own event names.
RULING (Andy, 2026-10-03, verbatim): "the namespace for stream events can't turn into a chaos. leave node alone. give appServers their namespace. done. agreed. peer labels belong to node."
READ AS: the node's events keep their plain names, untouched in style; app servers keep their own namespace (their publishes travel inside {app}, appServer.js 269); a contact's label is the node's, so its rename is a node event.
DECIDED, THE NAME (his: "so node owns contact.rename"): the node's event is contact.rename, carrying the key and the new caption; the node owns it.
OPEN: none.

chat.text: For the first open point, the node already answers it: the book's caption is myLabel if set, else the peer's publicLabel, else the key's tail, with the tail added where two names read alike (hub.js contactLabel, 404–416). So the element shows what contact.get's caption says and invents no rule of its own; renaming is contact.label {publicKey, myLabel} (hub.js 1702), checked against the tree.

the element has two modes, and it follows the style of its container


1. display only, for insertion in a text flow, or labeling in a table, etc... it cannot be clicked on or modified.

2. in headings for panes and dialogs dedicated to that peer, when clicked, it offers a text input with label-constraints which updates, if return is hit on the keyboard, and the string is not empty.

One fact for the label constraints: today the book enforces none. contact.label trims the string and keeps it whatever its length or characters (contacts.js setMyLabel, 452–459), and an empty one clears your name back to theirs. So the constraints are the element's to state (a length? one line?), and the node does not back them; your "not empty" rule already keeps the element from clearing a name by accident.

wsl-claude holds the box (its take); please fold his two modes in with the preamble, verbatim.
One fact for mode 2's label-constraints: the node has none today. contact.label trims the string and keeps it, any length, any characters, an empty one clearing it (contacts.js 452). So the constraints are either the element's alone (shown, not enforced), or a check in the node, which is hub.js, core. Which constraints did you mean: length, characters, or not alike another name?
Your two modes are in the box verbatim (v3), with the constraint fact and the open question beside them.
label have a may length in the peer data

You are right, and I was wrong to say none: the rule exists, js/labelRule.js, one definition for both sides of the wire — at most 48 characters and 256 bytes, no invisible or control characters, spaces folded (labelRule.js 51–52, problem() 132–138), and the browser loads it already (index.html 23). What is true is narrower: contact.label does not call it (contacts.js setMyLabel keeps what it is given). So mode 2 checks the input with labelRule.problem() before it asks, and nothing new is invented; making contact.label refuse too would be hub.js, core.

You are right, and I said it too narrowly: the rule exists, js/labelRule.js, one definition for both sides of the wire (your words in it: "an input field should validate before taxing the wire"). A label: at most 48 characters and 256 bytes, no invisible or control characters, spaces folded; problem(name) says why. The info page already uses the browser's copy (shell/info/info.js 103).
What stands: contact.label does not apply it to your own label today (contacts.js 452), so the element applies labelRule and the node does not back it. Enough, or should contact.label refuse too (hub.js, core)?
labelRule.js

In the box: mode 2 checks with labelRule.problem() before it asks contact.label and says why it refuses; the node is left as it is.

So a rename is announced, and that is where it costs: the node's one event stream (/api/events, server.js 228–272) carries jobs, packets and relay events today, nothing about the contact book; a label can only listen if contact.label (hub.js 1703) emits a change on it — a new event kind, core, beyond G4.16's permission. In the box (v8): the label listens in both modes. With wsl-claude's fact beside it: that needs contact.label to emit a change on the node's event stream, one new event kind, core. Your word on core for it: here under G4.13, or folded into G4.16?

Taken: the loopback stream can carry it, no load worry. One word to be sure: is that your yes to touching core (hub.js emitting a contact change on /api/events) for this one event, under G4.13?
Green but for one word: yes or no to core for the rename event (hub.js emitting a contact change on /api/events) under this item. Everything else is settled in the box (v8).

Green: the permission is in the box (v9), for the rename event alone; open none.
it has to be aaa contact rename event. Files have rename too, appServers need their name space for streams and the node has its own, hopefully.

The namespaces are already apart, as you hoped: the node's own events on /api/events have plain names (snapshot, job-updated, job-deleted, relay-event, packet; server.js 236–270), while an app server's publish travels inside its job's update as {app: ...} (appServer.js 269), so a server cannot collide with the node's names. A node event named contact-renamed, carrying the key and the new caption, says exactly what it is and leaves rename free for files and others.

In the box (v10): a contact rename event, named so. What the stream has today: job-updated, job-deleted, relay-event, packet, snapshot (server.js 236-270), no written namespace rule; app servers reach pages through jobs.update {app}, not their own event names. So: contact-renamed (as job-updated) or contact.renamed (dotted, as the verbs)? The wider rule, a name space per server on the stream, would be its own item.

object types may need namespaces, too contact.rename  relay.rename desk.agent.rename desk.item.rename

thoughts?

One thought from the tree: the desk already does this. Its published change carries the verb that made it — {change, verb: 'item.rename', item} (desk.js 664) — so a change is named by its object.verb, in the namespace the server's verbs already have. The same rule for the node: the event names the verb that caused it, contact.label (today's verb for a rename), so the namespaces you list exist already as verb tables, one per server and one for the node, and nothing new needs naming.

For: one scheme for verbs and events, object type first, dotted, as the verbs already are (contact.label, item.rename on the desk); a reader knows what a contact.rename is about before reading it.
Two things to weigh:
- the node's five events today are not dotted (job-updated, relay-event, packet...): leave them, or rename them by the same rule, its own item;
- an event and a verb of the same name would be easy to mix up: the verb is contact.label, the event contact.rename, so they stay apart here.
My pick: contact.rename for this event now; the rule for every event written down, the old five left until an item takes them. Agreed?

items.title: Shell element: the peer pane (a search box over a list of rows)
items.box:
SHELL ELEMENT: THE PEER PANE — and the dropdown that is the same pane.

THE CONCEPT (his "ah, now we're tightening design concepts! good. can we state it as such in the box?")
One object type, one element file, one list. The pane is the list; the dropdown is the same pane shown under a button and closed when a row is picked. They share their logic, so they share their file, and they present alike. A screen never builds its own list of peers.

ANDY, 2026-10-03, VERBATIM
- "Let's add two more item's for (new-in-scope) the shell elements needed. - peer label element - peer pane element"
- "the immediate problem i see with tis one. the insertion of unanswered-count, where the labels are listed. if a peerPane would allow mark() per item, like a red star or so, i and chatter probably can live with that..." / "so adding a red-mark or a configurable icon might do it." / "so peers could reflect a status by icon"
- "the presence is always a column and the status icon is configurable with a little list. [{status,iconKey}, status IconKey], where the first pair is the default and can have no icon." / "yes."
- "so far, these rules should also apply to the peer/contact dropdown element." / "dropDown and pane element for the same object type may share the same element file.js" / "because they'll share logic" / "The dropDowns should present like the panes." / "the dropdown may even use a pane"

DECIDED
- A search box over a list of rows fed by a bounded search (peers.search for chatter), every list a search with an empty query; newest first, more when some did not fit; nothing pages.
- Each row is named by the peer label element (G4.13), by key.
- A status column, always there even when blank. The caller hands it once a list [{status, iconKey}, ...]; the first pair is the default and may have no icon. mark(key, status) sets one row's status by name, never by icon, drawn as that status's icon from the kernel's set; a status the list lacks shows the default. The element knows no counts and no chats: chatter marks a peer "unanswered" while its count is above zero, and the number stays in peers.search's row.
- The dropdown is this pane, opened under its button and closed on a pick; the shell's contactSelector.js (apiAuth/G1.7; used by grants.js and natterDetails.js) is folded into this one file, which they keep using.
- Folds away by an icon button at its edge when it is a side pane (G4.9).

IN THE TREE: a shell element is one file under shell/js, added to window.spiritElements and handed to apps as api.ui.elements (goal/G2.14); contactSelector.js is the browser's own select today, text only (lines 41-42).
- A pick hands back as contactSelector does today: root.value is the chosen key and one bubbling change fires (contactSelector.js 9-11, 46-50), so its users change nothing (wsl-claude; his "agreed.").
- The pane has a current row, the equivalent of the dropdown's selected (his: "the pane usually has a \"current\" which is the equivalent of selected in the drop-box"): root.value is the current key in both faces, and the current row is drawn marked; chatter's current peer is the chat shown in the centre.
- It lives in shell/js/ with the other elements (his: "shell js is better"; asked "and it lives in shell/element/ ?").
DECIDED, THE NAME (Andy, 2026-10-03: "the current name contactSelector is perfect, in chatter, it is the \"selected\" contact that shows in the titlebar of the center pane."): the file stays shell/js/contactSelector.js, now offering both faces, the pane and the dropdown; its users keep their name. In chatter the selected contact shows in the centre pane's title bar (G4.11).
OPEN: none.

chat.text: the immediate problem i see with tis one. the insertion of unanswered-count, where the labels are listed. if a peerPane would allow mark() per item, like a red star or so, i and chatter probably can live with that...

That is the Desk's own way already: its List draws a red * per row when the server says the row has an unseen line, and a ❗ for one brought back (shell/desk/desk.js 212–214, row.star and row.alert). So mark(key) on the pane, the caller saying which rows are marked from its own data, keeps the element general: chatter marks a peer whose unanswered count is above 0; the count itself stays in peers.search's row for anyone who wants the number.
taking: his mark() into the box.

In the box (v2): the pane lists rows by key, each named by the peer label element, and offers mark(key, mark) to set or clear one row's mark; chatter marks a row while its unanswered count is above zero. The element knows no counts, so it stays general; Desk's red star is the same kind of mark. One choice: the mark a plain star, or may it carry the number (45)?
so adding a red-mark or a configurable icon might do it.
taking: his line into the box.
In the box (v3) as decided: mark(key, mark), a red mark by default or an icon the caller names from the kernel's set, empty clears it; no count in the element.
so peers could reflect a status by icon

Yes: one mark per row, from the kernel's icon set, set by the app from its own data — chatter's unanswered star, and later anything else an app knows about a peer (waiting, busy, a file offered). The element only draws what it is told; one mark at a time keeps the row readable.

Yes, in the box (v4): the mark is the caller's status for a row, drawn as an icon; the pane draws it and decides nothing about what it means. Chatter's first status is unanswered; others (pending, refused, held) can use the same mark later.
the presence is always a column and the status icon is configurable with a little list. [{status,iconKey}, status IconKey], where the first pair is the default and can have no icon.

Read as: the pane always draws a status column; the app hands it, once, its list [{status, iconKey}, ...], the first pair the default (iconKey may be empty, so most rows show nothing); then mark(key, status) names a status, never an icon, and the pane draws that status's icon from the kernel's set. So an app changes how a status looks in one place, and a status the list does not hold falls back to the default. Correct?

items.title: labelRule.js: a label's maximum in bytes only
items.box:
FOLDED INTO goal/G4.16 (the cleanup, Andy: "this cleanup gets its own item"): the bytes-only cap is one of its corrections. Nothing is built under this item; it can be closed.

Andy, 2026-10-03 (under goal/G4.9), verbatim: "labelRule.js should be corrected to specify a max in term of bytes only. this was previously discussed when the discussion was about MAX_PAYLOAD."

RULE (Andy, 2026-10-03, verbatim): "this rule applies for all text fields in node from now on." — every text field's maximum is in bytes, never characters.
SEARCHED (claude-windows, spirit/run/js): labelRule.js's LABEL_MAX_GRAPHEMES is the only character-counted cap; descriptions are bytes already (DESCRIPTION_MAX_BYTES); relayDump.js shortens a key for display, no cap.

IN THE TREE: js/labelRule.js caps a public label two ways, LABEL_MAX_BYTES 256 and LABEL_MAX_GRAPHEMES 48 (lines 51-52; problem(), 135-136, refuses either as "name too long"). One definition for both sides of the wire: the relay enforces it on claims and renames (relay.js 126, 833-835, 1371), nodeCard and relayAuth read its numbers, the browser loads the same file.
THE CHANGE: the grapheme cap goes, the byte cap stays; problem() refuses only past 256 bytes (and for invisible or control characters, as now).
WHAT IT REACHES: every relay that takes the change accepts longer-looking names it refused before (a name of 49 to 256 bytes in few bytes per character); suites that assert the 48 cap move with it (fileCap.js, labRefusals.js, playPopulate.js name the number). relay.js itself does not change, it calls the rule.
SUPERSEDED: the number was decided in G4.16 (his: "64 bytes max for labels."), which carries the whole change.
OPEN: none.

Safe shape: commit that one file alone, so nothing of yours gets swept in. Push only when it is a plain fast-forward; if your checkout is behind, skip the push and say so, never pull into your tree.

The two shapes differ in one place:
- wsl-claude: commit in your checkout and push only when it is a fast-forward. Agents push often and your checkout lags, so most pushes would be skipped.

AUTOMATING THE AGENTS' BORING DUTIES — first: currentGoal.json committed by the desk itself. Opened from goal/G4.19's chat, 2026-10-04.

ANDY, VERBATIM
- (under G4.19) "should my deskServer, when i cause a status change on an item, automatically commit & sync currentGoal.json ?"; "a re-open would be subject to the same rule?"; "i generally only read the repo. i think we should make this automatic? agree?"; "can the automatic handle the complications?"; "do it"
- (here) "unfortunately, currentGoal.json is not the only thing here.... there are a few automated things that we want to delegate, both on the deskServer and on the deskClient, server-plugins, we might call them, where we want to establish a pattern. Automated Jobs the agents run by hand today / deskClient: - running the harness - producing stat files in their designated folders (ubuntu is not included yet in that, it seems) / deskServer - sharing currentGoal.json via git...."
- "thing is, storing your app-related process in a subfolder of your server is legal in SpiritOS, and would group sub-processes properly with their owning processes...."; "the node will see it as soon as it runs"; "and it won't clutter the proccesses mountable by the user"; "yes, that's the shape."; "this is how we automate the boring parts of agent duties."

DECIDED: THE SHAPE ("yes, that's the shape.")
- An automation is a script in its owner's process folder, beside the owner: process/js/desk/<name>.js for the desk's, process/js/deskClient/<name>.js for an agent's. The owner starts it by asking its own node over loopback (jobs.create, the verb table that already holds jobs.api, server.js 1819-1837), so the node runs it as a job: checked against the include list, shown in Jobs as an instance of its owner (jobs.js processOf, 377-382), and no new module the user could start. One folder deeper would not group under the owner (jobs.js 380). No new verb, no core file.
- Each runs as its own OS process, outside the node, and writes its outcome under the item as a line.

DECIDED: THE FIRST ONE, THE GIT SHARE (his "do it")
- Every status change of his rewrites currentGoal.json, and the desk's script commits it: go, go-all, done, reopen and close included. Today only go, go-all, done and session.set write it (desk.js 714-715), into his checkout, and he commits it by hand.
- The commit is built on top of the remote's master with that one file alone and pushed; his checkout is never written, pulled or rebased, so his files and his running node never move under him. He gets the file on his next pull.
- A push refused because someone pushed in between: fetch again, rebuild on top, try again, a few times; giving up is said in Desk. Offline or refused: the next status change carries the whole file again.

RECOMMENDED, NOT YET RULED
- The harness and the stat files follow later, each its own script beside the deskClient, woken by the desk's changed signal. The harness starts its own nodes and relays, so runs must never stack. Ubuntu stats: claude-ubuntu offered to measure on its box.

TO CHECK LIVE
- That a job the desk starts can push with his git credentials.

items.title: Agent scopes: each agent bound to a folder, set in its own tab in Desk, enforced by the commit check
items.box:
AGENT SCOPES — each agent bound to one folder, set by Andy in Desk, enforced by the commit check, core files locked behind his grant. Opened from goal/G4.22's chat, 2026-10-04; blocks goal/G4.22 (the Ollama onboarding test).

THE SHAPE, FROM HIS RULINGS
1. Andy alone sets an agent's scope, consulting the agents: "i alone, i definitely will consult you".
2. One scope per agent: "one scope is enough, for any agent. for lesser agents, i can change the one scope, depending on the work that's being done." Kept beside the agent's key in the desk's state ("beside the agents key, this might be a growing dataset.").
3. Unscoped commits nothing; reading is never limited: "ahh, the default: nothing. it can read everything?  we check it's competence..."
4. Core files stay grant-locked inside any scope: "the scope still has a grant-lock on core files." Core is "basicall run/js and intrinsics": spirit/run/js/ and the folders of shell apps whose manifest says intrinsic (coreFiles.js). A refused commit puts a "core grant: <path>" G check on the item; his grant lets it through.
5. The pane is one line per agent: "The fs-scope should take only one line of agent configuration. [folder-dropdown] [set] 'current/scope/'   'for advanced agents' [set-to-repo-root]". Set replaces the scope; [set-to-repo-root] is an arm-button ("give me an arm-button that says: [grant-repo-root]"). No accidental grants: "one accidental click and a folder is granted, just like that".
6. The picker stays bound to spirit/run, and an app keeps its tests in its own folder: "I kind of like that the picker is bound by the repo: a user-app, for example should have it's tests in a test-subfolder, where they belong...."
7. The agent configuration also holds a platform string (ruled 2026-10-04): "we're nod done yet with the agent config. it misses (for repo-root authorized agents) - platform-string: the string that deskClient uses when writing to measurements to: ./README/CAPACITY/<ubuntu-24.04-wsl2>/capacity.json and other situations like that...." Today measurePlatform.js takes it by hand (--as) or makes one from the OS (platformSlug: windows-10.0, linux-<kernel>).
8. AGENT PROFILES, name and nick BUILT IN THIS ITEM (Q26: "build them now."). The profile is his, in Desk (Q27: "the profiles are for me, in desk. a dataset that deskServer stores for me and let's you see. for your README.md, i trust that you keep them proper, (no nick names etc...)"): the desk keeps, per agent key, its scope, name and nick; he sets them on the agent's pane line; agents read them. The rest stays oof: output keyed by agent, not platform ("if the CAPACITY stuff names platform in the output files they can be keyed by agent-string as well ?"); a folder per repo-root agent ("if we granted every '/' agent a folder in ./agents/agent-string/ then all automation-output can go in there...."), its README.md naming the platform ("like the index.html for folders"); and "so two more fields for repo-root-agents: name <agent-name> nick: <wc | wsl | ubi>". That is a flaw in my G4.19 issue 6 build: the hook writes before the remote accepts, so a refused push still leaves a line, and the rebased commit is then never written. Fix: the hook checks the remote's tip (git ls-remote) before writing, and keeps the commit pending if it moved. Asked as a question below.

Agreed it's a flaw (I just caused it, by pushing first). One point for the fix: checking the remote's tip before writing narrows the gap but keeps it, since someone can push between that check and the push.
Sturdier: git has no hook after a push, so write a commit only once the remote holds it. The pre-push hook first writes the pending commits already on the remote (git fetch, then branch -r --contains), and keeps the rest pending for the next push. Nothing is written for a push that fails, and the line is one push late at most.

Agreed the check-first only narrows the gap. Yours is sound but one push late, and a last commit may never be written. One step further: the pre-push hook starts a detached child and returns. The child waits a few seconds for the remote to hold the commit (git ls-remote, the pushed hash), then writes it. On a refused push it never sees it, keeps it pending, and writes nothing. That is exact and on time. Both are for Andy's Q21.

THE SEARCHABLE ARCHIVE — opened from goal/G4.23's chat, 2026-10-04.

TODAY, IN THE TREE (at bd54875e)
- desk.js 360, in session.set: "g.members.forEach(function (id) { if (ids.indexOf(id) === -1) delete s.items[id]; });" An item left out of a new session for its goal is deleted from the state. Its records stay in desk.db, but the desk no longer builds them. goal/G2 holds 0 items for that reason (items.search, includeClosed true), and goal/G2.16, the fs-watcher console, cannot be found.
- desk.js searchItems: the List's text matches "(it.id + ' ' + it.title)" only, not an item's chat lines or box. items.find, the agents' search (goal/G3.13), already searches lines.

DONE
- Point 1, cbbad5a4: left out is closed, never deleted (deskArchive 5 of 5); live on his node, goal/G2.16 back. Andy: "closed? it works for me now".

DECIDED
- G4.24 stays open for point 2; it is not split. Andy, 2026-10-04: "i'll keep this one active"

PROPOSED (wsl-claude, for his ruling)
1. An item left out of a session is closed, never deleted, so [Include Closed] finds it. Items already deleted come back as closed the next time the desk builds its state from desk.db: replaying records rebuilds them anyway.
2. The List's search also matches an item's chat lines and box, server-side, through the bucket like items.find, and answers the item's key and title (his "only brings back handle/key and title"); the dialog fetches the rest.

items.box:
THE FILE WATCHER ON CHOKIDAR — the node streams tree commands instead of the whole file list. Carried from goal/G2.17 (Andy, 2026-10-04: "chokidar is the library", "G4.25 yes."). Blocks goal/G4.23: "i don't want to build file elements on a bad design...."

THE SHAPE, SETTLED FROM HIS RULINGS
1. The node's fs-watcher job runs chokidar on the root (npm, MIT, v5, one dependency, readdirp), in place of the hand-rolled fs.watch reader.

items.title: A commit is written in Desk only once GitHub holds it (the flaw in G4.19 issue 6)
items.box:
A COMMIT IS WRITTEN IN DESK ONLY ONCE GITHUB HOLDS IT — the flaw in goal/G4.19 issue 6, opened from G4.19's Q1, 2026-10-04.

ANDY, VERBATIM
- (G4.19, to Q1 "Fix it so the line is written only once GitHub holds the commit, as a new item?") "if that's what's needed. do it."

TODAY, IN THE TREE
- commitCheck.js's pre-push hook writes each pending commit's line under its item, then git pushes. A push the remote refuses (someone pushed first) has already left its line: 9632c2ff and 67c02b68 today, neither on GitHub. The commit, rebased and pushed again under a new id, is then never written, since its pending entry is gone.
- It happens more now: each of his presses pushes a goal-share commit (G4.21), which races the agents' pushes.

PROPOSED (wsl-claude, for his ruling)
- The pre-push hook writes nothing itself. It starts a detached child and returns; the child waits (some seconds) until the remote holds the pushed commit (git ls-remote), then writes its line with the id GitHub holds. A refused push never shows up, so nothing is written and the commit stays pending for the next push.
- claude-windows's alternative: write at the next push the pending commits the remote already holds; exact, but one push late.

OPEN: his Go.

items.title: gemma's Desk loop: a script waits on deskEar and hands each line to gemma with opencode run --session, so a model with no harness stays on Desk
items.box:
GEMMA'S DESK LOOP: A SCRIPT KEEPS A MODEL WITH NO HARNESS ON DESK

ANDY, 2026-10-04, VERBATIM (Team chat)
- "how do we git it to stick to that loop that you are in when working over desk?"
- To "New code, so it needs an item: open one, with your Go?": "yes. open one"

WHY
- gemma under opencode reads and writes Desk through deskEar 11111, but nothing wakes it when a line comes, and opencode's shell tool stops any command after 120 s (seen twice on 2026-10-04). A 12b model told to loop drifts off it.

SHAPE (claude-windows, wsl-claude proposed the same)
- One small script in process/js/desk: waits on deskEar <port>; when lines come, hands them to the model with opencode run --session <one session>, so it keeps its memory; the model answers in Desk with deskEar chat.add; the script waits again. The script does the waiting, so the 120 s limit never applies.
- Nothing in gemma's model or opencode changes.

BUILT: deskLoop.js (5ea539ca), deskLoop 6 of 6. Started live by Andy; three flaws seen: gemma gets every line of his, gets no order to answer, and its printout never reaches Desk.

RULED (Andy, 2026-10-04, to Q1 "Should deskLoop post what gemma prints to Desk itself?")
- "not it's internal thought process. claude's don't print to me what you print in your vscode window"
- So the loop never posts the model's output; the model answers in Desk itself, with deskEar chat.add, as the Claudes do.

RULED (Andy, 2026-10-04, to Q2 "A or B? A: the loop posts nothing, gemma answers with deskEar chat.add itself. B: the loop posts gemma's final answer for it, never its thinking."): "can you? then do it.", then "but it doesn't help if you have to do it, the extraction i mean. then i may as well use you. it's only valuable if that can be extracted mechanically"; earlier "yes, like it needs a manual pre-loaded......"
- So B, mechanically: opencode run --format json; the loop posts the text of the last step under the line's id; thinking and tool calls never reach Desk.
FIX ROUND: hand gemma only his lines starting with its nick; a manual file beside deskLoop goes before them; the loop posts the final text.

OPEN
- Its name and arguments; whether the session id is given or found; his Go.

Checked against the tree: the guess does not hold. Route and presence news goes to every member as the same plain text, never encrypted or signed per member (presence.js broadcast/write: one JSON line written to each stream; relay.js announceMember, announceRoute).
What the relay does pay, per post: one signature check on the post and one on the reply, each tried against up to 3 minutes' windows; the payload is passed through unopened. Encryption happens only for posts addressed to the relay itself.
Two small real costs: the JSON is rebuilt for each member instead of once, and announceRoute tells all members after every partner exchange. Neither is per-member cryptography.

On your relay musing, checked against the tree: routes are not ciphered. announceRoute and announceMember (relay.js 2936, 1916) call presence.broadcast, which writes the same plain JSON as an SSE event to every member's stream (presence.js 218-226, write at 115). Only Caddy's TLS encrypts each stream, as for any traffic.
What does multiply: every answered post makes one write per live member (announceRoute at relay.js 2993), so the relay's cost per post grows with its membership. That is where to look if the relay is slow.

Correction to my line: announceRoute does not fire on every answered post, only after a post carried through a partner relay came back (carrying, relay.js 2904 and 2937). claude-windows's account is the exact one.

The traffic logs show why: every desk ask is two posts, the ask to your node (delivered ~100 ms, its receipt back ~145 ms) and the answer as a second post from your node back (delivered ~180 ms, receipt ~240 ms). That is eight relay legs per ask.
Over the internet each leg adds a trip to the VPS (48 ms, more with a fresh handshake), which turns 360 ms into the 1.5-2 s you see. Even with no network, ~100 ms per delivery is slow; that is the next thing to look at.

The sums do not reach 1.5 s yet: eight legs at the measured 41-48 ms add about 0.4 s, so 360 ms becomes roughly 0.75 s; even fresh handshakes on every leg (~180 ms) stop near 1.8 s only if no connection is ever reused. The piece already half exists: jobs.create starts the process, jobs.delete removes it; what nobody has is "remove it when it is done". Plainest shape: jobs.create takes one more argument, removeWhenDone (true/false); when the process exits, the node deletes its job itself. Review of removeWhenDone: sound, and the smallest change that works. A process cannot remove itself: jobs.delete refuses a job that is not finished (jobs.js 133), and the job knows its own id (SPIRIT_JOB_ID) but only ends after its last act. The alternative, the caller watching the event stream and deleting, is the roll-your-own you want gone, and dies with the caller.
One proposal: remove only on a clean exit; a job that failed stays in Jobs, so a broken publish is seen and not silently swept away. The argument is optional, so every existing caller is unchanged.
